html:
The Brushed Pottery culture was an archaeological culture of eastern Lithuania, Belarus and southeastern Latvia, from the late Bronze Age through the early Iron Age, roughly the first millennium BCE into the first centuries CE.

It is named for its pots: flat-bottomed vessels whose outer surface was roughened with strokes, probably made with bundles of straw or grass while the clay was wet. It followed the Neolithic Narva culture in the region.

Its people lived mostly on hillforts, small fortified settlements on hills and river bends, with wooden houses inside earth ramparts. They grew grain, raised cattle, pigs and horses, and also hunted and fished. Iron, smelted from local bog ore, came into use over these centuries.

They are generally seen as ancestors of the eastern Balts, and so in time of the Lithuanians and Latvians. The culture bordered the Milograd culture to the south, the Dnieper-Dvina culture to the east and the coastal peoples, such as the forebears of the Curonians, to the west. In the early centuries CE it gave way to the East Lithuanian barrows, from which the medieval Lithuanian tribes grew.
sum: The Brushed Pottery culture was an archaeological culture of eastern Lithuania, Belarus and southeastern Latvia, from the late Bronze Age through the early Iron Age, roughly the first millennium BCE into the first centuries CE.
